Using power responsibly

A reading is not yet a prediction.

A reading that fits a text is not yet evidence that it predicted an event.

A closer lookOpen in a larger view ↗

The interactive example has its own motion control. Scroll inside it if you need more room.

A proposed way to test interpretations of texts

Start with the passage, when it was written and what it claims. Then ask what separate evidence there is for the event it describes.

The research keeps these questions apart. It also asks whether an interpretation works on cases that were not used to invent it. This room makes no forecast and gives no personal prophecy.

Open each kind of evidence. Notice why one does not automatically establish the next.

Words used here
held-out test
Trying a rule on examples that were not used to develop or choose it.
Read the fuller explanation

The prophetic-admissibility pilot distinguishes literary fit, a narrative’s own account of fulfilment, independently dated outcomes, held-out validation and theological attribution. Each is a different claim. An exact calculation at one rung cannot silently promote the reading to the next.

The catalogue deliberately includes uncertain candidacies and names traditions still outside its coverage. Membership means a passage deserves examination as future-directed language; it does not establish supernatural truth, fulfilment or predictive reliability.

Inspect the evidence questions on the desk. There are no dates to optimize toward, no forecast of your future and no personal reading. The aim is a disciplined encounter with interpretation and its alternatives.
